question_en: Which solid waste rules apply to my homestay now? I heard the 2016 rules were changed.
answer: Yes, the Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 were replaced by new Solid Waste Management Rules 2026. They were notified in January 2026 and came into effect on 1 April 2026. They apply to both urban and rural local bodies. Small homestays mainly need to follow the four-bin sorting at source.
actions: Sort your waste into four streams: wet, dry, sanitary and special care.
Ask your Gram Panchayat how it will collect each stream.
Keep a copy of the PIB summary or ask the District Pollution Control office for the rule text.
evidence: PIB release: rules supersede SWM Rules 2016, effective 1 April 2026; PIB releases give the notification date as 27 or 28 January 2026 (they differ)
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board / Gram Panchayat / District Collector office
caution: Exact notification date differs between PIB releases, so only the month is stated. Full rule text was not opened; check the gazette.

question_en: What are the four types of waste I have to separate at my homestay?
answer: The 2026 rules ask for four-stream sorting at source. Wet waste is kitchen waste, vegetable and fruit peels, meat and flowers. Dry waste is plastic, paper, metal, glass, wood and rubber. Sanitary waste is used diapers, sanitary pads, tampons and condoms. Special care waste is paint cans, bulbs, mercury thermometers and medicines.
actions: Keep four clearly marked bins or bags in the kitchen, rooms and washroom area.
Put a short picture sign above the bins in Hindi or your local language.
Tell guests about the bins at check-in.
evidence: PIB release lists the four categories with examples
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / urban local body
caution: Local bodies may use their own colours or bin names. Ask what your village follows.

question_en: Is my homestay a 'bulk waste generator' and do I need to register?
answer: Under the 2026 rules a bulk waste generator meets any one of these: floor area of 20,000 square metres or more, water use of 40,000 litres a day or more, or 100 kg of solid waste a day or more. A normal village homestay is far below these numbers. So it is very unlikely to be a bulk generator. You still must sort your waste.
actions: Estimate your daily waste weight for a few days to be sure.
Ask your Gram Panchayat if any local rule covers small hotels or resorts.
evidence: PIB release: thresholds 20,000 sq m floor area OR 40,000 L/day water OR 100 kg/day waste
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board
caution: A large resort, camp or event venue could reach these limits. State boards may add their own rules.

question_en: Who is supposed to collect waste in my village, and what if no garbage van comes?
answer: Under Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen) Phase II, the Gram Panchayat arranges waste collection and a village segregation shed, often using women Self Help Groups. Plastic goes door to door to the shed and then to a Plastic Waste Management Unit through block or district officials. How well this works differs by village. If no van comes, raise it with the Sarpanch and Gram Panchayat secretary.
actions: Write a short request to the Gram Panchayat asking for a collection day and a drop point.
Ask the Panchayat if your village has a segregation shed and an SHG that runs it.
Store dry waste clean and dry until it can be handed over.
evidence: SBM-G Phase II document: GP roles for plastic, biodegradable waste, greywater; SWM Rules 2026 apply to rural local bodies
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / Block Development Officer / District Swachh Bharat Mission cell
caution: Document is from 2023. What exists in your village depends on the state and the Panchayat.

question_en: Where do I throw plastic when no garbage van comes to my village?
answer: Do not burn or bury plastic. Keep it dry and apart from wet waste. Ask the Gram Panchayat for the village segregation shed or Plastic Waste Management Unit drop point. If there is none, agree a regular handover day with the Panchayat or an SHG, or carry clean dry plastic to the nearest town collection point.
actions: Collect dry plastic in a covered sack away from the kitchen.
Ask the Gram Panchayat where the nearest drop point is and who takes it.
Write the answer on a card for your guests so they use the same place.
evidence: SBM-G Phase II: GP collects plastic to village segregation shed then PWM units; SWM 2026 dry waste stream. The advice not to burn is general practice
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / Block office
caution: Burning plastic gives off harmful smoke. Check whether your state also has a specific burning ban.

question_en: How can I deal with kitchen and food waste in my village homestay?
answer: Wet waste should be sorted at source and composted or sent for biogas. Under SBM-G, biodegradable waste is segregated into dry and wet at source and treated at household or community level. In a village you can use a compost pit, a vermicompost bed or feed suitable scraps to your own livestock. Keep meat and cooked food away from open pits to avoid flies and animals.
actions: Dig or build a covered compost pit away from the well and kitchen.
Keep a separate caddy for peels and food scraps inside the kitchen.
Ask your Krishi office or Gram Panchayat for a vermicompost or compost demonstration.
evidence: SWM 2026 wet waste stream composted or biomethanated; SBM-G biodegradable waste management at household/community level. Pit placement advice is general practice
verify_with: Block agriculture officer / Gram Panchayat
caution: Place pits well away from drinking water sources and streams.

question_en: What is GOBARdhan and can my farm waste make gas or fertiliser?
answer: GOBARdhan is a scheme under Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen), launched in 2018. It turns cattle dung, crop residue, kitchen waste and market waste into biogas and bio-slurry (manure). As of 27 January 2026 the government reported 189 working Compressed Bio-Gas projects and 979 community or cluster biogas projects. Individual farms can also look at household biogas plants under MNRE.
actions: Ask the Gram Panchayat if a GOBARdhan project or cluster plant exists nearby.
Check the MNRE biogas programme if you keep cattle and want a household plant.
Plan how guests can see the plant safely if it becomes a visit.
evidence: PIB GOBARdhan release (figures as of 27 Jan 2026); MNRE biogas page
verify_with: District Water and Sanitation Mission / MNRE state nodal agency
caution: Availability depends on your district. Biogas pits need safety rules around gas and children.

question_en: Is there government help to install a biogas plant at my home or farmstay?
answer: MNRE runs a biogas programme for rural households and farms. For small plants of 1 to 25 cubic metres per day, the page shows central help from Rs 9,800 to Rs 70,400 per plant, depending on size. Some groups such as SC/ST beneficiaries, North Eastern Region, islands and registered gaushalas get extra support. Apply on the Biogas Portal.
actions: Count your cattle and daily dung to choose a plant size.
Register interest on the MNRE Biogas Portal or ask your state nodal agency.
Ask what rules apply if the plant also feeds a guest kitchen.
evidence: MNRE Biogas Programme page as read on check date
verify_with: State renewable energy agency / MNRE Biogas Portal
caution: Subsidy amounts can change. Confirm before you buy. This is the amount stated on the page, not a promise.

question_en: Can I burn leaves, paper or plastic waste behind my homestay?
answer: Do not burn plastic, sanitary waste or mixed waste. The smoke harms your family, guests and neighbours. Dry leaves and garden waste are better composted or mulched. I could not confirm the exact burning ban or fine in the 2026 rules, and states may have their own rules. Ask your Gram Panchayat or State Pollution Control Board.
actions: Compost or mulch garden waste instead of burning it.
Keep plastic dry and hand it to the village collection point.
Ask the Panchayat if there is a local ban or fine on open burning.
evidence: Burning ban not verified in SWM Rules 2026 summaries read; advice is general practice
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board / Gram Panchayat
caution: Do not state a fine amount to guests unless the local authority confirms it.

question_en: What do I do with used sanitary pads and diapers from my guests?
answer: Sanitary waste (used diapers, sanitary towels, tampons, condoms) is its own stream under the 2026 rules. Keep it separate from wet and dry waste in a covered bin in the washroom. Do not flush it or burn it. Ask the Gram Panchayat how sanitary waste is taken in your village.
actions: Place a covered, lined bin in every guest washroom and show it with a picture sign.
Wrap used items in paper or a bag before they go in the bin.
Ask the Gram Panchayat how and when sanitary waste is collected.
evidence: SWM Rules 2026 four-stream list names sanitary waste: used diapers, sanitary towels, tampons, condoms
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / ASHA or Anganwadi worker / State Pollution Control Board
caution: Respect guest privacy. Use gloves when emptying the bin and wash hands after.

question_en: How do I get rid of old medicines, bulbs, thermometers and paint tins?
answer: These belong to the 'special care' stream in the 2026 rules: paint cans, bulbs, mercury thermometers and medicines. Do not mix them with wet or dry waste, and do not burn or bury them. A separate summary of the rules also lists pesticide containers and used batteries, but I could only confirm the first list on the PIB page. Ask your Gram Panchayat where these are collected.
actions: Keep a separate closed box for special care items.
Take expired medicines to the nearest health centre or ask the Panchayat for a collection route.
Never reuse empty pesticide containers for water or food.
evidence: PIB release lists paint cans, bulbs, mercury thermometers, medicines as special care waste
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / Primary Health Centre / State Pollution Control Board
caution: Broken bulbs or thermometers can release mercury. Keep children away and ask the local health worker.

question_en: Can our hill village charge tourists a fee for waste management?
answer: The 2026 rules include special provisions for hilly areas and islands. According to the PIB release, local bodies there can levy user fees on tourists and regulate tourist numbers based on available waste management facilities. How this works in practice is decided by the local body and the state. A village cannot start a fee on its own without the proper body approving it.
actions: Discuss the idea in the Gram Sabha and record the decision.
Ask the Block Development Officer or district tourism office how a fee can be approved.
Use the fee only for waste work and report to the community.
evidence: PIB release: user fees on tourists and regulation of tourist inflow in hilly and island regions
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / District Collector / State urban or rural development department
caution: Amounts, receipts and who collects must follow local rules. Do not charge informal fees.

question_en: What happens if I do not follow the waste rules?
answer: The 2026 rules provide for environmental compensation for non-compliance such as operating without registration, false reporting, forged documents or improper solid waste management, enforced by pollution control boards. I could not confirm fine amounts for a small village host. Local bodies may also have bye-laws with fines.
actions: Ask your Gram Panchayat or district pollution office which fines apply to small hosts.
Start sorting waste and keep a simple note of where each stream goes.
evidence: PIB release: environmental compensation for non-compliance, no amounts for small generators
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board
caution: Do not quote fine amounts unless you have them in writing from the authority.

question_en: What do I do with farm waste, crop stalks and animal dung when guests are staying?
answer: Do not burn crop stalks if you can avoid it. Use them as mulch, animal feed, compost or biogas feed. GOBARdhan treats cattle dung, crop residue and kitchen waste as resources. Keep dung heaps away from guest rooms, wells and streams, and cover them to reduce smell and flies.
actions: Place the dung heap or compost downwind and away from guest areas and water.
Turn stalks and leaves into compost or mulch.
Tell guests when animal work happens so they can choose to see it or avoid it.
evidence: GOBARdhan release names animal waste, kitchen leftovers, crop residue and market waste as inputs. Placement advice is general practice
verify_with: Block agriculture officer / Veterinary officer
caution: Crop residue burning is restricted in some states. Ask your state agriculture or pollution board.

question_en: What do I do with leftover used cooking oil from frying?
answer: Do not pour used oil into drains, soak pits or streams. FSSAI runs a RUCO (Repurpose Used Cooking Oil) initiative that links food businesses to collectors who turn used oil into biodiesel. I could not open the FSSAI page this session, so ask the food safety officer how to join. The food safety topic covers more detail.
actions: Store used oil in a closed container away from the stove.
Ask the District Food Safety Officer about RUCO collectors in your area.
Never sell used oil to someone who will resell it for cooking.
evidence: FSSAI RUCO page could not be read this session (fetch failed); pointer only
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI RUCO
caution: Re-using oil too many times is unsafe for health. Follow FSSAI advice.

question_en: Which single-use plastic items are banned, and does it apply to my homestay?
answer: Since 1 July 2022 India bans identified single-use plastic items. The list includes ear buds with plastic sticks, plastic sticks for balloons, plastic flags, candy sticks, ice-cream sticks, thermocol (polystyrene) for decoration, plastic plates, cups, glasses, cutlery such as forks, spoons and knives, straws, trays, wrapping or packing film around sweet boxes, invitation cards and cigarette packets, PVC banners below 100 micron, and stirrers. It applies to everyone, including hosts and shops.
actions: Switch to steel, glass, leaf plates, clay cups or bamboo straws for guests.
Remove banned items from your stock and ask suppliers for alternatives.
Check your state, which may have a stricter list.
evidence: PIB release of 1 July 2022 ban list as read; some items summarised
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board / District Collector
caution: State rules may add more items. Ask the State Pollution Control Board for the current list.

question_en: What thickness of plastic carry bag is allowed for my craft shop?
answer: Plastic carry bags below 75 microns were prohibited from 30 September 2021. Bags below 120 microns have been prohibited from 31 December 2022. Many states ban plastic bags completely, and cloth, jute and paper bags are safer choices. Do not rely on thickness alone, because your state may not allow any plastic bags.
actions: Offer cloth, jute, paper or reusable bags to buyers.
Ask your State Pollution Control Board if plastic carry bags are fully banned in your state.
Remove thin bags from the shop.
evidence: PIB release: below 75 micron from 30 Sep 2021, below 120 micron from 31 Dec 2022
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board
caution: Compostable bags may also be restricted in some states, for example Kerala.

question_en: Can I use thermocol plates or plastic cups for a village feast for guests?
answer: Plastic plates, cups, glasses and cutlery are on the national banned list, and so is thermocol for decoration. Thermocol cutlery is banned in Himachal Pradesh with fines. Use leaf plates (patal), steel plates, earthen cups and washable cutlery instead. For big feasts, set up a simple wash point.
actions: Collect steel plates and cups from the community for events.
Buy leaf plates (sal, banana, areca) from local makers.
Ask guests to bring their own bottle and cup.
evidence: PIB SUP list; HP notification 6 July 2018 on thermocol cutlery
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board
caution: Check whether paper cups with plastic lining are allowed in your state.

question_en: What is EPR for plastic and does it affect a small host?
answer: EPR (Extended Producer Responsibility) means companies that make or import plastic packaging, and brand owners, must take responsibility for collecting and recycling it. The EPR guidelines for plastic packaging were notified on 16 February 2022. Small hosts are not the producers. Your part is to sort plastic waste so it can be recycled and to ask suppliers for less packaging.
actions: Buy in bulk or refill packs from local suppliers.
Keep clean dry plastic separate for the village recycling system.
Ask suppliers whether they take back packaging.
evidence: PIB release on EPR guidelines notified 16 Feb 2022 under PWM Amendment Rules 2022
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board
caution: Obligated categories were not listed in the release read.

question_en: Are shampoo sachets and small packets allowed in my homestay rooms?
answer: Sachets are not named in the national single-use plastic list I read, but your state may have its own rules. They are hard to recycle and often end up in the village drain or field. Refillable dispensers or soap bars cut waste. Ask your State Pollution Control Board if your state restricts them.
actions: Use wall-mounted refill dispensers for soap and shampoo.
Buy local soap bars or reuse bottles that you wash.
Ask the Panchayat whether sachets can be recycled in your area.
evidence: National SUP list read does not name sachets; state rules not checked
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board
caution: This is a practice suggestion, not a legal ruling.

question_en: Can I sell or give packaged water bottles to guests?
answer: There is no national ban on packaged water bottles that I could verify. Some places restrict them, so ask locally. In Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh the single-use plastic bans cover many items, and a few tourism areas push refill stations. I could not confirm an official Sikkim bottled water order this session. Offer filtered or boiled water in refillable bottles to cut plastic.
actions: Ask the District Tourism Office if bottles are restricted where you work.
Set up a clean refill point with a safe water source.
Sell steel or glass bottles as a local product.
evidence: No official bottled-water ban order was read; Sikkim claim only from news snippets (not read)
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board / District Tourism Office
caution: Do not tell guests an official ban exists unless the authority confirms it.

topic: How to check my state plastic rule
question_en: How do I find out what plastic is banned in my own state?
answer: National rules set the minimum, and many states go further. A July 2024 statement to Parliament lists state-wise bans, such as complete carry bag bans in Sikkim and Himachal Pradesh. Ask your State Pollution Control Board, District Collector office or Gram Panchayat for the latest order.
actions: Visit or call the District Pollution Control office and ask for the plastic ban order.
Ask the Gram Panchayat for the local notice.
Print the list and put it in your host guide.
evidence: PIB-hosted Parliament statement July 2024; national list PIB 2022
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board
caution: The 2024 statement may be outdated. Confirm each state rule with the board.

question_en: I run a homestay in Himachal. What plastic and thermocol rules apply, and what are the fines?
answer: Himachal Pradesh has a long list of bans under its Non-Biodegradable Garbage (Control) Act 1995, including plastic carry bags since 2009, disposable plastic cups, glasses and plates since 2011, thermocol cutlery since July 2018, and a wider list of single-use items notified on 20 July 2022. The 2018 notification covers hotels, dhabas and banquet halls. Compounding fines in that notification range from Rs 500 for up to 100 g to Rs 25,000 for over 10 kg, with Rs 1,000 for individual littering and Rs 5,000 for institutional littering.
actions: Use steel, glass or leaf tableware and cloth bags.
Stop stocking thermocol cutlery and plastic disposables.
Ask the HP State Pollution Control Board for the current fine table.
evidence: HP notification 2018 (fine table) and HPPCB reply to NGT 2024 (dates and fine table)
verify_with: Himachal Pradesh State Pollution Control Board
caution: Fine amounts are from the 2018 notification and the 2024 board statement. They may change.

question_en: What plastic rules apply for homestays and treks in Uttarakhand?
answer: A statement to Parliament lists a 2017 Uttarakhand notification banning plastic carry bags, cups, bowls, containers, tumblers, glasses and plates made of plastic or thermocol. A 2023 Uttarakhand Pollution Control Board report says plastic is banned in forest areas such as sanctuaries and reserves, and mentions a Rs 500 refundable deposit on certain treks returned when plastic is brought back. The report also notes littering fines in Kedarnath. Check current details with the board.
actions: Do not carry plastic cutlery, plates or thermocol into forest areas.
Ask the trek or forest office about deposit systems.
Tell guests the rules before the trek.
evidence: PIB-hosted Parliament table (2017 notification); UKPCB 2023 workshop report
verify_with: Uttarakhand Pollution Control Board / Forest Department
caution: The 2023 report is a workshop report. Trek deposit rules differ by trek.

question_en: What are the plastic rules in Ladakh and what are the fines?
answer: On 19 June 2026 Ladakh banned the use, sale, storage, supply and transport of identified single-use plastic items, including cutlery, cups, plates, straws, trays, wrapping films, thermocol decorations, plastic flags, stirrers and thin banners. The page states fines of Rs 10,000 for single-use plastic violations and Rs 5,000 for littering. It applies to individuals, hotels and eateries, and random checks are planned at Leh airport and entry points.
actions: Remove banned plastic items from your stock and kitchen.
Tell guests at booking not to bring plastic cutlery or plates.
Keep a refill water point and steel bottles for guests.
evidence: Ladakh UT page dated 19 June 2026
verify_with: Ladakh Tourism Department / Ladakh Pollution Control Committee
caution: Confirm the latest notification before you quote fines to guests.

question_en: What plastic rules should a Sikkim homestay follow?
answer: A July 2024 Parliament statement lists a complete ban on sale, use and storage of plastic carry bags in Sikkim, effective 4 June 1998. Sikkim has also been in the news for restrictions on packaged water and thermocol, but I could not open an official order for those this session. Check with the Sikkim State Pollution Control Board.
actions: Use cloth or jute bags in your homestay shop.
Ask the Sikkim State Pollution Control Board about bottled water and thermocol orders.
Keep your own filtered water for guests.
evidence: PIB-hosted Parliament table: Sikkim carry bag ban 04-06-1998; bottled water and thermocol not verified
verify_with: Sikkim State Pollution Control Board
caution: Do not quote bottled-water or thermocol rules as fact until confirmed.

question_en: What plastic items are banned in Kerala and Goa for a homestay or guesthouse?
answer: A July 2024 statement to Parliament says Kerala has a complete ban on single use plastic and plastic carry bags, including compostable plastic, through notifications dated 27 November 2019 and January and February 2020. For Goa it lists a ban on making, stocking, selling and using plastic carry bags, cups, forks, paper plates and spoons and other non-biodegradable items under an amendment dated 8 August 2019. Confirm current rules, since court orders can change them.
actions: Use cloth, jute, steel and glass items.
Ask the Kerala or Goa State Pollution Control Board for the current list.
Remove banned items from rooms and kitchen.
evidence: PIB-hosted Parliament table July 2024
verify_with: Kerala State Pollution Control Board / Goa State Pollution Control Board
caution: Statement is from 2024. Court orders and notifications may have changed things.

question_en: What plastic rules apply to homestays in Meghalaya?
answer: A July 2024 Parliament statement lists a partial ban in Meghalaya on use and sale of plastic bags below 50 microns (notification dated 16 February 2017). The national single-use plastic ban list also applies. District rules may be stricter, so ask the Deputy Commissioner.
actions: Follow the national banned item list for plates, cups and cutlery.
Ask the Deputy Commissioner's office or Dorbar Shnong about local rules.
Use bamboo, cane and cloth alternatives.
evidence: PIB-hosted Parliament table (Meghalaya partial ban); national SUP list
verify_with: Meghalaya State Pollution Control Board / Deputy Commissioner
caution: Village councils (Dorbar Shnong) may also set local rules. Respect them.

question_en: How do I stop trekkers from leaving waste on the trail my village uses?
answer: The simple rule is 'pack it in, pack it out'. Leave No Trace is an international good-practice code, not an Indian law. Uttarakhand has used a refundable Rs 500 deposit on certain treks that is returned when plastic waste comes back. Weigh or count items at start and finish, and make your guides responsible for the group's waste.
actions: Give each trekker a bag and note items taken out.
Count plastic at the start and finish of the trek.
Ask the forest or tourism office if a deposit or checkpoint system is possible.
evidence: LNT principle 3 'Pack it in, pack it out'; UKPCB 2023 mention of Rs 500 refundable deposit on certain treks
verify_with: Forest Department / District Tourism Office
caution: Leave No Trace is a good-practice code. Local trek rules come first.

question_en: What do I do with old phones, chargers, TVs and fans from my homestay?
answer: Under the E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022, in force since 1 April 2023, collection and processing of e-waste can only be done by registered producers, recyclers and refurbishers. Unregistered informal operators can face closure and seizure. Do not break open or burn old electronics. Give them back to the seller, a registered collector or ask the Panchayat or nearest town about a collection point.
actions: Store old electronics in a dry box away from children.
Ask the seller of the new item to take back the old one.
Search for a registered collector through the district pollution board.
evidence: PIB release on E-Waste Rules 2022 in force 1 April 2023
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board / CPCB e-waste portal
caution: Consumer duties were not spelled out in the release read. Burning cables or batteries releases toxic smoke.

question_en: How do I dispose of inverter batteries, solar batteries and used cells?
answer: The Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 cover electric vehicle, portable, automotive and industrial batteries. Producers and importers must collect and recycle waste batteries, and landfill and incineration are not allowed. Do not dump or burn batteries. Return old batteries to the seller or a registered recycler when you buy a new one.
actions: Give the old battery to the dealer when you buy a new one.
Store used batteries upright in a dry place until pickup.
Ask the district pollution board for a registered recycler.
evidence: PIB release on Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 (published 24 August 2022)
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board / battery dealer
caution: Lead acid batteries leak acid. Wear gloves and keep children away.

question_en: What do I do with used bandages, gloves and needles from first aid at my homestay?
answer: Used bandages with blood and any needles should not go in the normal bin or be burned. Use gloves, double bag the dressings and keep sharps in a hard closed container. Then take them to the nearest Primary Health Centre and ask how they handle them. I did not verify the exact bio-medical waste rule for households, so please confirm with the health centre.
actions: Put used dressings in a sealed bag and sharps in a hard plastic bottle.
Wash hands well after handling them.
Ask the Primary Health Centre or ANM what they accept.
evidence: General first-aid hygiene practice; Bio-Medical Waste Rules page not read
verify_with: Primary Health Centre / District Medical Officer
caution: Do not try to treat serious injuries yourself. Go to the nearest health centre or call the local emergency number.

question_en: What is IS 10500 and how do I know if my drinking water is safe for guests?
answer: IS 10500 is the Bureau of Indian Standards specification for drinking water. The edition I could confirm is IS 10500:2012 (Second Revision). It lists limits for taste and look, chemicals and bacteria. It has 'acceptable' and 'permissible' limits, and acceptable limits are the safe target. You cannot tell water is safe by looking or tasting it. Get it tested.
actions: Ask the Pani Samiti or Jal Jeevan Mission office for your latest test report.
Get your own source (borewell, spring, tank) tested at an approved water lab.
Share the result with the Panchayat if it fails.
evidence: BIS IS 10500:2012 PDF read (title, edition, scope); acceptable and permissible limit idea is from a news commentary (secondary), numbers not extracted
verify_with: BIS / District Public Health Engineering or Jal Shakti water lab
caution: I did not verify numeric limits and I could not confirm whether a newer edition than 2012 is in force. Ask the lab for the limit it uses.

question_en: Where can I get my village water or borewell water tested?
answer: Government water testing labs are meant to be open to the public, and the Jal Jeevan Mission framework says samples can be tested at affordable rates. Villages also have trained community members who use field test kits for a first check. Ask the Pani Samiti, the Block office or the PHED (Public Health Engineering Dept) lab.
actions: Ask your Gram Panchayat who the five trained women with field test kits are.
Take a clean sample bottle to the nearest district or block water lab.
Keep the test report in your host file.
evidence: JJM WQMS Framework: labs opened to public at affordable rates; FTK training of five women per village
verify_with: District PHED / Jal Shakti Water Quality lab
caution: Lab names and fees differ by state. Ask what bottle to use and how to collect the sample.

question_en: What is the field test kit in my village and who uses it?
answer: A Field Test Kit (FTK) is a portable kit for a first check of water quality. Under Jal Jeevan Mission, trained members of village water committees, Self Help Groups and volunteers use it, and results go to the JJM water quality portal. By 12 March 2026 about 24.8 lakh women had been trained. The kit is a screening, not a replacement for lab tests. The JJM framework says village surveillance should be at least monthly.
actions: Ask the Panchayat for the names of trained women in your village.
Request a test of your supply before the tourist season.
Ask what the result means before you tell guests.
evidence: PIB FTK release 16 March 2026; JJM WQMS Framework
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / Pani Samiti / PHED
caution: FTKs give a first screening only.

question_en: What if the village tap water test shows contamination?
answer: The JJM framework says that when contamination is found, the water supply agency should shut off the contaminated supply and provide safe alternative water. Tell guests not to drink the tap water until it is safe. Ask for the test result and a written action plan from the Pani Samiti or PHED, and inform the health worker.
actions: Switch guests to a tested safe source or boiled and cooled water.
Report the result to the Sarpanch and PHED in writing.
Ask for a re-test after the fix.
evidence: JJM WQMS Framework: shut off contaminated supply and provide alternative
verify_with: Pani Samiti / PHED / Block Medical Officer
caution: If guests have stomach illness, send them to a health centre and report it to the health authority.

question_en: How much chlorine should be in drinking water and can I chlorinate my tank myself?
answer: WHO guidance says residual chlorine at the point where people collect water should be between 0.2 and 0.5 mg/l, with at least 30 minutes contact time at 18 degrees or warmer. Cloudy water needs clearing first, because turbidity should be below 5 NTU for chlorine to work. Do not guess doses. Ask the Pani Samiti, JJM operator or health worker for the correct method for your tank.
actions: Ask the JJM operator or health worker to show the dosing and a DPD test.
Clean and rinse the storage tank before disinfection.
Test free chlorine and note the date.
evidence: WHO Technical Note 11: 0.2 to 0.5 mg/l at point of consumption; 30 min contact at 18 C+; turbidity below 5 NTU
verify_with: PHED / JJM operator / Health worker
caution: This is WHO guidance for supplies, not a BIS rule. Too much chlorine is also unsafe. Do not mix chemicals yourself.

question_en: Is boiling enough or do I need a water filter for guests?
answer: Boiling and filters can each help but they do not fix every problem. Boiling helps against germs, but not against chemicals such as fluoride, arsenic or high nitrate. Filters differ in what they remove, and some need electricity or regular care. First get the water tested, then ask a health or water officer which treatment suits your problem.
actions: Test the source water before you buy a filter.
Choose treatment based on the test result, not on advertisement.
Clean filters on schedule and keep a log.
evidence: General practice; official health guidance on household treatment not read this session
verify_with: Health Department / PHED
caution: Do not tell guests water is safe if you did not test it.

question_en: My borewell water has iron, fluoride, arsenic or is hard. What should I do?
answer: These are chemical problems that boiling does not remove. The JJM framework mentions special arsenic test kits in affected areas. Do not give such water to guests or use it for cooking until it is checked and treated. Ask the PHED or Jal Shakti department which community treatment plant or safe source your village can use.
actions: Get a lab test that includes fluoride, arsenic and iron.
Ask PHED for a safe supply or community treatment plant.
Use a safe alternative for drinking and cooking.
evidence: JJM WQMS Framework: arsenic FTK; IS 10500 covers chemical limits (numbers not verified)
verify_with: PHED / District Health Officer
caution: Long term exposure to fluoride or arsenic can harm health. Seek medical advice if symptoms appear.

question_en: Do I need a CGWA NOC (permission) to use a borewell for my homestay?
answer: Under the groundwater guidelines (24 September 2020, amended 29 March 2023), individual domestic users for drinking water are exempt from an NOC. Hotels and resorts fall under 'commercial use', and the guidelines did not show a small-size exemption for them in what I read. Whether a small village homestay needs an NOC depends on the state authority and the amount you draw. Ask your State Ground Water Authority.
actions: Note your borewell depth, pump power and daily water use.
Call the State Ground Water Authority or district office and ask in writing.
Do not drill a new borewell for guests before getting an answer.
evidence: CGWA consolidated guidelines PDF read via summary: individual domestic drinking users exempt; hotels under commercial use; exact clauses to be checked
verify_with: Central Ground Water Authority / State Ground Water Authority
caution: Rules differ by state authority. Details were read through a tool summary, so verify the clauses.

question_en: I have a farm borewell. Do I need NOC if I add a farmstay?
answer: The guidelines read say agricultural activities are exempt from the groundwater NOC. Once you also supply water for paying guests, that part may count as commercial use, and the answer can change. Keep farm and guest water use separate on paper and ask the state authority how it treats farmstays.
actions: Write down how much water the farm uses and how much the farmstay uses.
Ask the State Ground Water Authority in writing about farmstay water.
evidence: CGWA consolidated guidelines: agriculture exempt, hotels under commercial use
verify_with: State Ground Water Authority
caution: This is not a legal ruling. Confirm with the authority.

question_en: How can I start rainwater harvesting at my homestay and is it required?
answer: Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain asks citizens to harvest rain 'where it falls, when it falls'. It also promotes renovating traditional water bodies and recharging groundwater. The 2016 Model Building Bye Laws say buildings on plots of 100 sq m or more must include a rainwater harvesting plan when plans are sanctioned, but states and local bodies decide how they apply, and village rules may differ. Rooftop water for washing or gardens is a good start.
actions: Collect roof water in a clean tank or recharge pit.
Keep rooftop water separate from drinking water unless treated.
Ask the Gram Panchayat about Catch the Rain support or MGNREGA water work.
evidence: PIB Jal Shakti Abhiyan page; PIB release on Model Building Bye Laws 2016 (100 sq m plots)
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / Block office / local building authority
caution: Rainwater from roofs needs filtering and treatment before drinking.

question_en: Can I use the village spring for my guests, and who must I ask?
answer: A village spring or stream is usually a shared source with local customs and rules. Using it for paying guests can reduce what the village has, especially in the dry season. Ask the Gram Panchayat, Pani Samiti or village council before using it for the business. Record the decision and share it with the community. I cannot give the exact legal rule without your state and site.
actions: Raise the question in the Gram Sabha or village meeting.
Agree how much water the homestay may use and when.
Write down the agreement and review it each season.
evidence: General practice and community consent principle; no single source
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / Village council / Pani Samiti
caution: Water rights and customary rules differ by state and community.

question_en: What if my village runs short of water in the dry season while guests are here?
answer: Plan for it before the season. Limit guest numbers to what your water can support, store rainwater, fix leaks, and tell guests how to save water. Never take water from the village supply if the village is short. Agree with the Panchayat how the village comes first. Meters and a simple daily log help you see how much you use.
actions: Check your water use per guest night in the dry months.
Install low-flow taps and fix leaks.
Tell guests at booking that water may be limited.
evidence: General practice; HWMI water measurement (S21); Catch the Rain (S124)
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / PHED
caution: Community needs come before tourism use.

question_en: Is it okay to buy tanker water for my homestay in summer?
answer: I could not verify a national rule about private tankers. Check where the tanker water comes from and whether taking it affects other villages. Ask for the source, get the water tested, and store it in a clean covered tank. Do not use tanker water for drinking unless it is tested and treated.
actions: Ask the tanker supplier for the water source and test report.
Clean the tank before refilling and keep it covered.
Tell the Panchayat if tanker supply is part of your plan.
evidence: General practice; no official source read
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / PHED
caution: Tanker water quality varies widely.

question_en: How do I keep children and guests safe around an open borewell or well?
answer: Cover every borewell and well with a strong, fixed cap or fence. If you stop using a borewell, ask the local authority how to seal it properly. Never leave one open, even for a short time. I did not read the official Supreme Court or state guidelines this session, so check the local rule.
actions: Check all borewells and wells on your land today and fix caps.
Put a visible warning and keep children supervised.
Ask the Panchayat how abandoned borewells are sealed locally.
evidence: General safety practice; official borewell guidelines not read
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / District Administration
caution: If a child or person falls in, call the emergency number and the district administration at once. Do not try risky rescues.

question_en: How do I measure how much water my homestay uses per guest?
answer: Read your meter at the same time each morning for a week and write it down. If there is no meter, use a bucket test, tank level markings or pump run-time times flow rate. Divide the total by guest nights to get litres per guest night. This number is your baseline. Use it to check improvements.
actions: Write the meter reading in a notebook each morning.
Count guests each night and divide litres by guest nights.
Repeat each month to see changes.
evidence: HWMI water measurement approach (S21) and UNEP tourism water and waste guidance (S26); Indian village adaptation is general practice
verify_with: Local trainer / District Tourism Office
caution: Estimates from a bucket or tank are rough. Use them only to compare over time.

question_en: What does 'ODF Plus' mean for my village and my homestay?
answer: ODF Plus is a Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen) level for villages that keep open defecation free (ODF) status and also manage waste. 'Aspiring' means solid or liquid waste arrangements, 'Rising' means both, and 'Model' also means visual cleanliness (little litter, no stagnant wastewater, no plastic dump in public places). A clean ODF Plus village is a strong base for tourism, and the Gram Panchayat leads the work.
actions: Ask the Gram Panchayat which ODF Plus level your village has.
Help with litter clean-ups and wastewater arrangements near your homestay.
Use the ODF Plus status in your guest information only if the Panchayat has confirmed it.
evidence: SBM-G Phase II document defines ODF Plus Aspiring, Rising and Model
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / District Water and Sanitation Mission
caution: Do not claim ODF Plus status for your village unless it is officially declared.

question_en: Where should the dirty water from my kitchen and bathrooms go?
answer: SBM-G prefers simple on-site solutions near the source, such as soak pits, leach pits, magic pits or watering a kitchen garden. Where space is short, communities may use community systems such as waste stabilisation ponds or constructed wetlands. Do not let greywater run into streams, wells or the lane. Pass it through a grease trap or filter first.
actions: Make a soak pit or kitchen garden for kitchen and bathroom water.
Fit a simple grease trap or filter on the kitchen drain.
Keep soak pits away from wells and springs.
evidence: SBM-G Phase II document: GPs promote soak pits or kitchen gardens near the source
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / Block sanitation officer
caution: Pit size and distance from water sources depend on soil. Ask the local engineer.

question_en: Can guests wash clothes or use soap in the stream or spring near my homestay?
answer: Avoid washing with soap or detergent in or beside streams, springs or wells, even if the soap is called 'natural'. Soap harms water life and the water people drink downstream. Collect water in a bucket and wash and drain well away from the source into a soak pit or garden. This is good practice, and local rules may also apply.
actions: Tell guests where to wash and where not to.
Provide a washing area connected to a soak pit.
Keep a sign near the spring explaining the rule in simple words.
evidence: Leave No Trace principle on waste disposal (practice, not Indian law); no Indian rule read
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / Pani Samiti
caution: Community rules about springs come first.

question_en: Should my new guest toilets use a septic tank or a twin-pit system?
answer: SBM-G promotes twin leach pit toilets in many villages, where waste turns into manure over time. States and local bodies also set rules for septic tanks. I could not verify the BIS septic tank standard this session. The right choice depends on soil, water table, space and number of guests. Ask the block engineer or sanitation officer before you build.
actions: Ask the Block sanitation engineer which design suits your plot.
Keep toilets away from wells and springs.
Plan for emptying and safe disposal before you build.
evidence: SBM-G Phase II (twin-pit and FSM roles); PIB FSM release Jan 2026; BIS standard not read
verify_with: Block Development Officer / District sanitation cell
caution: Do not discharge toilet waste into drains, fields or streams.

question_en: Who empties my septic tank and where does the sludge go?
answer: Faecal sludge management (FSM) is part of SBM-G. Districts run operations, and Gram Panchayats help with mechanised desludging and twin-pit retrofitting. Do not empty tanks by hand or dump sludge in fields or streams. Ask the Panchayat or the district Swachh Bharat cell for an authorised desludging service and where the waste is treated.
actions: Call the district sanitation cell or Panchayat for an authorised service.
Note the date of emptying and keep the receipt.
Never let anyone enter a tank. Gas can kill.
evidence: SBM-G Phase II document and PIB FSM release (6 Jan 2026)
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / District Swachh Bharat Mission
caution: Manual cleaning of septic tanks is dangerous and not allowed. Use trained workers with proper equipment.

question_en: Are dry or composting toilets allowed in cold hill villages with little water?
answer: A January 2026 PIB release lists ecosan toilets used in Leh, Ladakh, in extreme cold, and twin-pit retrofitting in Sikkim as examples of rural sanitation models under SBM-G. Whether a dry or composting toilet is accepted for a homestay depends on your state and district. Ask the sanitation cell for approved designs and how to handle the compost.
actions: Ask the district sanitation cell about approved designs for your altitude.
Visit a working ecosan toilet and learn how it is managed.
Train staff on safe handling and cleaning.
evidence: PIB release 6 January 2026 naming Leh ecosan toilets and Sikkim twin-pit retrofitting
verify_with: District Swachh Bharat Mission / State rural sanitation department
caution: Guest toilets need privacy, light and handwashing. Do not use untreated compost on food crops without advice.

question_en: Can I dump waste or build near a lake, wetland or river in my village?
answer: For notified wetlands, the Wetlands Rules 2017 prohibit solid waste dumping, discharge of untreated waste and effluents from villages and other settlements, encroachment and setting up industries. Permanent construction is restricted, and the State or UT Wetlands Authority enforces. Not every lake is notified, so ask. Never dump waste or discharge untreated water in any water body.
actions: Ask the District Forest Office if your lake or wetland is notified.
Do not build, dump or discharge near it without permission.
Include a no-dumping rule in your guest briefing.
evidence: Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2017, Rule 4 as read
verify_with: State Wetlands Authority / District Forest Officer
caution: Rules apply to notified wetlands. Other water bodies may be protected by state or local laws.

question_en: Can I get a subsidy for rooftop solar on my homestay under PM Surya Ghar?
answer: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana is for households. As stated in a PIB release (Feb 2024), the subsidy is Rs 30,000 for 1 kW, Rs 60,000 for 2 kW and Rs 78,000 for 3 kW or more, capped at 3 kW. Eligibility asks that the applicant be an Indian citizen, own a house with a suitable roof, have a valid electricity connection and not have taken another solar subsidy. It is aimed at residential homes, so a separate commercial building may not qualify. Check the portal.
actions: Ask your electricity company (DISCOM) if a homestay in your own home counts as residential.
Check current rates on the PM Surya Ghar portal before applying.
Get quotes only from vendors listed on the national portal.
evidence: PIB release PRID 2010757 (subsidy per kW and eligibility); July 2026 PIB release confirms scheme running
verify_with: Electricity distribution company (DISCOM) / pmsuryaghar.gov.in helpline
caution: Subsidy amounts may have changed since the Feb 2024 release. Whether homestays count as residential is not stated. Ask.

topic: Star labels and solar water heater
question_en: How do I choose efficient appliances and a solar water heater for my homestay?
answer: The BEE star label shows how efficient an appliance is, and more stars generally means less electricity for the same job. For hot water, solar water heaters can replace electric geysers where there is sun. I could not open the BEE or MNRE pages this session, so I cannot give subsidy details. Ask your state renewable energy agency about approved solar heaters.
actions: Choose appliances with more stars when you replace them.
Replace old bulbs with LED bulbs and tube lights.
Ask the state renewable energy agency about solar heater schemes.
evidence: General practice; BEE and MNRE pages not read this session
verify_with: BEE / State Renewable Energy Development Agency
caution: Do not quote subsidy amounts without confirming them.

question_en: Can I use my Ujjwala LPG connection in my homestay kitchen for guests?
answer: PM Ujjwala is a scheme for adult women from poor households. It gives a free LPG connection with a regulator, hose, first refill and a two-burner stove. The FAQ does not say that the connection can be used for a business, and the scheme is aimed at household cooking. Ask your gas agency before using a household cylinder for paying guests.
actions: Ask your LPG distributor about household versus commercial use.
Check which cylinder type your homestay is allowed to use.
Keep the cylinder in a ventilated place away from open flame.
evidence: PMUY FAQ page: eligibility and free items; commercial use not addressed
verify_with: LPG distributor / Oil marketing company
caution: Do not assume a household cylinder is allowed for commercial use.

question_en: My kitchen has a lot of smoke from the chulha. How can I protect guests and my family?
answer: Smoke from firewood and dung cakes harms lungs, eyes and children. Cooking with LPG or biogas is cleaner, and MNRE supports household biogas plants. If you must use a chulha, vent the smoke outside with a chimney, keep the kitchen separate from guest rooms and open windows. Do not let guests sleep near a smoky kitchen.
actions: Check if you can use LPG or biogas for daily cooking.
Fit a chimney or smoke outlet on the chulha.
Keep guest rooms away from the cooking area.
evidence: MNRE biogas programme and PMUY pages as read; ventilation advice is general practice
verify_with: Block office / MNRE state nodal agency / Health worker
caution: Smoke is a health risk. Never use charcoal or wood stoves in closed guest rooms.

question_en: Can I collect firewood from the forest for my guests' campfire or kitchen?
answer: Rules on collecting firewood or cutting trees differ by state and by forest status. In protected areas and reserved forests, collection can be restricted. Do not cut or collect without written permission or clear community rights. Ask your Forest Range Office or Van Panchayat or Joint Forest Management Committee.
actions: Ask the Forest Range Officer what you may collect and when.
Use fuel from permitted private or farm sources.
Avoid campfires for guests unless the forest office allows them.
evidence: General guidance; no forest rule read this session
verify_with: Forest Range Officer / Van Panchayat / JFMC
caution: Illegal felling and transit without permits can lead to penalties.

question_en: Can I run a diesel generator at night at my homestay? What are the noise limits?
answer: The Noise Pollution Rules set limits for residential areas of 55 dB(A) during the day (6 am to 10 pm) and 45 dB(A) at night (10 pm to 6 am). Industrial, commercial and silence zone limits were not visible in what I read. A running generator near rooms and neighbours will break calm nights. Place it away from guests, use a noise-cover and avoid night use.
actions: Move generators away from bedrooms and neighbours.
Avoid using the generator between 10 pm and 6 am.
Consider solar plus battery as a quiet option.
evidence: PIB release on noise standard: residential 55/45 dB(A) day/night; day 6 am to 10 pm
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board
caution: Silence zones near hospitals and schools have stricter limits. Check local orders.

question_en: Can I play music, use a DJ or sound firecrackers for a guest party at night?
answer: A PIB release on the Noise Rules says blowing of horns, bursting of sound-emitting firecrackers, operation of sound-emitting construction equipment and playing of bands should not happen at night, defined as 10 pm to 6 am. Loudspeaker rules and permissions are managed by the district authorities. Keep guest events short, indoors and quiet at night, and ask the local police or administration for rules.
actions: End music and amplified sound before 10 pm.
Ask the local police station or SDM office for loudspeaker rules.
Tell guests about quiet hours at check-in.
evidence: PIB releases on Noise Rules (night 10 pm to 6 am restriction on horns, firecrackers, bands as read)
verify_with: Local police / District Magistrate / State Pollution Control Board
caution: Local festivals may have special orders. Ask the authority for permission in writing.

question_en: How can I check how much electricity my homestay uses per guest?
answer: Look at the units (kWh) on your electricity bill, or read the meter on the same day each week. Divide monthly units by guest nights to get units per guest night. Compare busy and quiet months. The biggest use is usually water heating, cooling, pumps and old lights. Fix those first.
actions: Write the meter reading weekly in a notebook.
Note guest nights each month.
List your five biggest electricity uses and plan one change.
evidence: Adapted from HCMI (S15) and Carbon Trust hospitality energy guidance (S17); Indian bill reading is general practice
verify_with: Electricity company / local energy trainer
caution: Billing periods differ. Use the dates on the bill.

question_en: Is there a government guideline for ecotourism that our village can follow?
answer: Yes. The Ministry of Tourism's National Strategy for Ecotourism (April 2022) says communities are key stakeholders and most supplies and services should come from local providers. It adopts principles from the MoEFCC 2021 ecotourism guidelines, such as low-impact wildlife tourism, protecting ecological integrity, building environmental and cultural awareness and supporting local livelihoods. I could not open the MoEFCC 2021 document itself.
actions: Read the national strategy and note the points about community roles.
Ask the Forest Department which ecotourism guidelines your state follows.
Use the principles in your village tourism plan and record community agreement.
evidence: Ministry of Tourism National Strategy for Ecotourism 2022 as read; MoEFCC 2021 guidelines referenced there
verify_with: State Forest Department / State Tourism Department
caution: State ecotourism policies may add their own rules.

question_en: How many visitors can our village or trail take before it becomes a problem?
answer: The national ecotourism strategy asks for awareness of over-tourism, environmental impact and carrying capacity, and for monitoring visitor numbers, patterns and satisfaction. A fixed number is not given. Watch water use, waste, trail erosion and village life, then set a limit with the community. In hill areas, the 2026 waste rules also let local bodies regulate tourist inflow based on waste management facilities.
actions: Record visitor numbers each day for a season.
Ask the community which signs show 'too many'.
Set a daily limit and review it every season.
evidence: Ecotourism strategy text on carrying capacity and monitoring; SWM Rules 2026 hill-area provision per PIB
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / Forest Department / Tourism Department
caution: Limits for protected areas are set by the Forest Department, not by hosts.

topic: Entering forest or park with guests
question_en: Do I need permission to take guests into a forest, national park or sanctuary?
answer: Usually yes. Entry to national parks, sanctuaries and many reserved forests is controlled by the Forest Department, and permits, fees and registered guides may be required. The rules differ by state and by protected area. I did not verify the exact legal text this session. Ask the Range Officer or Park Director before you sell any trip.
actions: Contact the Forest Range Office and ask what permits and guides are needed.
Do not sell a trip into a protected area until you have written permission.
Ask if local community guides can be registered.
evidence: General guidance; Wild Life (Protection) Act text not fully read
verify_with: Forest Range Officer / Park Director
caution: Illegal entry or disturbing wildlife can lead to serious penalties.

question_en: Can I run a camp or bonfire for guests near a river, lake or forest edge?
answer: Camping and bonfires near water bodies, forests and protected areas are restricted in many places, and rules differ by state and site. For good practice, camp on durable ground away from water, use a stove where possible, keep fires small and legal, and carry out all waste. Ask the Forest Department, local authority and landowner before you set up.
actions: Get written permission from the landowner and the Forest or local authority.
Keep camps away from streams and use toilets that do not pollute water.
Do not light fires in dry season or in forest areas.
evidence: LNT principles 2 (durable surfaces) and 5 (minimise campfire impacts) as good practice; legal rules not verified
verify_with: Forest Department / District Tourism Office
caution: Campfire bans are common in fire season and in protected areas.

question_en: How do I avoid causing a forest fire and what do I do if one starts near my homestay?
answer: Forest fire season is usually the dry months, but dates differ by state. The Forest Survey of India sends satellite fire alerts by SMS and e-mail to registered users, and communities help through JFMCs, Eco-Development Committees and Van Panchayats. Do not light fires or throw cigarettes in dry forest, and tell guests this. If a fire starts, move people away, inform the forest office and local administration, and do not try to fight a large fire.
actions: Save the Forest Range Office and Van Panchayat numbers in your phone.
Ban open fires and smoking on dry trails during fire season.
Tell guests the fire rules at check-in.
evidence: PIB release: FSI alerts through SMS and e-mail; community role through JFMCs, EDCs, Van Panchayats
verify_with: Forest Range Office / Van Panchayat / District Disaster Management Authority
caution: Do not give exact fire season months unless your state forest department confirms them.

question_en: How close can guests go to wild animals and can they feed monkeys or deer?
answer: Never feed wild animals and keep a safe distance. Feeding makes animals lose fear of people and can lead to bites and conflict. Leave No Trace says to watch wildlife from a distance and never feed them. Inside protected areas, the Forest Department sets rules and a safe distance for each species. I could not verify any official distance numbers this session.
actions: Tell guests not to feed or tease any animal.
Store food and waste in closed containers to avoid attracting animals.
Ask the Forest Department for local rules and emergency contacts.
evidence: LNT principle 6 'Respect wildlife'; official distance rules not read
verify_with: Forest Range Office / Wildlife Warden
caution: Animals can be dangerous. If an animal is injured or aggressive, keep away and call the Forest Department.

question_en: Can guests pick flowers, herbs or take stones and wood from the trail as souvenirs?
answer: Ask guests to leave plants, stones and wood where they are. Leave No Trace says 'take photos, not souvenirs'. In forests and protected areas, collecting plants, herbs or wood may need permission and some species are protected by law. Do not let guests collect, and do not sell collected wild plants without checking the rules.
actions: Add 'look but do not take' to your guest briefing.
Ask the Forest Department which plants and products need permits.
Sell crafts made from permitted and sustainable materials.
evidence: LNT principle 4 'Leave what you find'; legal permissions not verified
verify_with: Forest Range Office / Biodiversity Management Committee
caution: Wild plant trade can fall under forest and biodiversity laws. Check before you sell.

question_en: What simple rules can I teach guests so we leave no trace on our trails?
answer: Leave No Trace has seven principles: plan ahead and prepare; travel and camp on durable surfaces; dispose of waste properly (pack it in, pack it out); leave what you find; minimise campfire impacts; respect wildlife; be considerate of others. This is an international good-practice code, not an Indian law. Local forest or village rules always come first.
actions: Print the seven rules in Hindi and local language for your guest card.
Tell guests the rules before every trek.
Add your local rules, such as no plastic and no loud music, to the card.
evidence: LNT 7 Principles page as read
verify_with: Local guide association / Forest Department
caution: Label this as good practice. Do not describe it as an Indian law.

question_en: What do the green, yellow, orange and red weather warnings mean and where do I check them?
answer: India Meteorological Department (IMD) bulletins use four colours. Green means no action, yellow means be aware, orange means be prepared to take action and red means take action. Check IMD forecasts for your district every morning in the season, and decide whether to move or cancel outdoor activities.
actions: Check the IMD district warning each morning in monsoon and winter.
Cancel or shorten treks on orange or red warning days.
Keep guests informed in simple words, without fear.
evidence: IMD bulletin colour code note as read
verify_with: India Meteorological Department / District Disaster Management Authority
caution: Warnings change. Follow the latest IMD and district notices.

question_en: What should I tell guests to do when lightning and thunder start on a trek or in the fields?
answer: NDMA advice: stay indoors if you can and avoid travel. If you hear thunder you are within striking distance. Do not shelter under trees, keep away from utility lines, metal fences, trees and hill tops, and do not lie flat on the ground. Keep children and animals inside. Hair standing on the back of your neck can mean lightning is near.
actions: Check the IMD forecast before outdoor activities.
Move guests to a low sturdy shelter early, and stay away from open ridges.
Teach your guides the NDMA lightning do's and don'ts.
evidence: NDMA lightning awareness page do's and don'ts
verify_with: NDMA / District Disaster Management Authority
caution: Do not wait for rain. Act at the first sound of thunder.

question_en: How should I plan for heat waves or cold waves when guests are staying?
answer: In heat, schedule outdoor activities for early morning or evening, keep water and shade ready, and watch children and older guests. In cold waves, keep rooms warm safely with ventilation, spare blankets and warm drinks. I could not open the NDMA public advice pages for heat and cold, so please use your district health office and IMD warnings.
actions: Check the IMD warning and district advisory every day in extreme seasons.
Keep drinking water, ORS and a first-aid kit ready.
Do not use charcoal or gas heaters in closed rooms.
evidence: IMD colour codes (S133); NDMA heat and cold wave advice not read, general practice
verify_with: District Health Office / NDMA / IMD
caution: Seek medical help if someone has heat stroke signs such as confusion or very high body temperature.

question_en: What should I do before the monsoon about floods, landslides and cloudbursts?
answer: Before monsoon, know your local risk, mark safe routes and meeting points, and save the district disaster control room numbers. Follow IMD colour warnings and local advice. Do not take guests across streams or below slopes during heavy rain, and cancel trips on red warning days. Ask the District Disaster Management Authority for local hazard maps and training. I did not verify local numbers.
actions: Ask the DDMA for your village hazard map and emergency numbers.
Plan an alternate route and a safe higher assembly point.
Cancel outdoor activities when heavy rain is forecast.
evidence: IMD colour code (S133); general disaster practice
verify_with: District Disaster Management Authority / Gram Panchayat
caution: Do not delay evacuation to save belongings. Move people first.

question_en: Are firecrackers or burning crop stalks allowed near my homestay?
answer: Rules on firecrackers and crop residue burning differ by state and district and change often. Night restrictions on sound-emitting firecrackers exist under the Noise Rules between 10 pm and 6 am. Crop residue burning is restricted in some states, especially around Delhi NCR. I did not verify a rule for your area. Ask your District Magistrate or State Pollution Control Board.
actions: Ask the district office for current firecracker orders before any event.
Use stalks as mulch or compost rather than burning them.
Choose lights and music over firecrackers for guest events.
evidence: PIB noise release for the night restriction; other rules not verified
verify_with: District Magistrate / State Pollution Control Board
caution: Do not rely on old orders. Check every year.
